The notebook helped Alex notice what had changed. A friend asked how they could help, and together they decided to make a simple plan. They listened to each other, checked what was possible, and left time to try again. This is demonstration text; the live library contains separate short readers.

data.title: Alice — demonstration excerpt
data.author: Lewis Carroll
data.notice: Original historical text: may contain dated language, prejudice, violence or distressing themes. Staff should review suitability.
pages:
CHAPTER I. Down the Rabbit-Hole

Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversations?”

So she was considering in her own mind (as well as she could, for the hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid), whether the pleasure of making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up and picking the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her.

There was nothing so _very_ remarkable in that; nor did Alice think it so _very_ much out of the way to hear the Rabbit say to itself, “Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!” (when she thought it over afterwards, it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this, but at the time it all seemed quite natural); but when the Rabbit actually _took a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket_, and looked at it, and then hurried on, Alice started to her feet, for it flashed across her mind that she had never before seen a rabbit with either a waistcoat-pocket, or a watch to take out of it, and burning with curiosity, she ran across the field after it, and fortunately was just in time to see it pop down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge.

In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.

The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then dipped suddenly down, so suddenly that Alice had not a moment to think about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very deep well.

Either the well was very deep, or she fell very slowly, for she had plenty of time as she went down to look about her and to wonder what was going to happen next. First, she tried to look down and make out what she was coming to, but it was too dark to see anything; then she looked at the sides of the well, and noticed that they were filled with cupboards and book-shelves; here and there she saw maps and pictures hung upon pegs. She took down a jar from one of the shelves as she passed; it was labelled “ORANGE MARMALADE”, but to her great disappointment it was empty: she did not like to drop the jar for fear of killing somebody underneath, so managed to put it into one of the cupboards as she fell past it.

“Well!” thought Alice to herself, “after such a fall as this, I shall think nothing of tumbling down stairs! How brave they’ll all think me at home! Why, I wouldn’t say anything about it, even if I fell off the top of the house!” (Which was very likely true.)

Down, down, down. Would the fall _never_ come to an end? “I wonder how many miles I’ve fallen by this time?” she said aloud. “I must be getting somewhere near the centre of the earth. Let me see: that would be four thousand miles down, I think—” (for, you see, Alice had learnt several things of this sort in her lessons in the schoolroom, and though this was not a _very_ good opportunity for showing off her knowledge, as there was no one to listen to her, still it was good practice to say it over) “—yes, that’s about the right distance—but then I wonder what Latitude or Longitude I’ve got to?” (Alice had no idea what Latitude was, or Longitude either, but thought they were nice grand words to say.)

Presently she began again. “I wonder if I shall fall right _through_ the earth! How funny it’ll seem to come out among the people that walk with their heads downward! The Antipathies, I think—” (she was rather glad there _was_ no one listening, this time, as it didn’t sound at all the right word) “—but I shall have to ask them what the name of the country is, you know. Please, Ma’am, is this New Zealand or Australia?” (and she tried to curtsey as she spoke—fancy _curtseying_ as you’re falling through the air! Do you think you could manage it?) “And what an ignorant little girl she’ll think me for asking! No, it’ll never do to ask: perhaps I shall see it written up somewhere.”

Down, down, down. There was nothing else to do, so Alice soon began talking again. “Dinah’ll miss me very much to-night, I should think!” (Dinah was the cat.) “I hope they’ll remember her saucer of milk at tea-time. Dinah my dear! I wish you were down here with me! There are no mice in the air, I’m afraid, but you might catch a bat, and that’s very like a mouse, you know. But do cats eat bats, I wonder?” And here Alice began to get rather sleepy, and went on saying to herself, in a dreamy sort of way, “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?” for, you see, as she couldn’t answer either question, it didn’t much matter which way she put it. She felt that she was dozing off, and had just begun to dream that she was walking hand in hand with Dinah, and saying to her very earnestly, “Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?” when suddenly, thump! thump! down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall was over.

Alice was not a bit hurt, and she jumped up on to her feet in a moment: she looked up, but it was all dark overhead; before her was another long passage, and the White Rabbit was still in sight, hurrying down it. There was not a moment to be lost: away went Alice like the wind, and was just in time to hear it say, as it turned a corner, “Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it’s getting!” She was close behind it when she turned the corner, but the Rabbit was no longer to be seen: she found herself in a long, low hall, which was lit up by a row of lamps hanging from the roof.

There were doors all round the hall, but they were all locked; and when Alice had been all the way down one side and up the other, trying every door, she walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she was ever to get out again.

Suddenly she came upon a little three-legged table, all made of solid glass; there was nothing on it except a tiny golden key, and Alice’s first thought was that it might belong to one of the doors of the hall; but, alas! either the locks were too large, or the key was too small, but at any rate it would not open any of them. However, on the second time round, she came upon a low curtain she had not noticed before, and behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high: she tried the little golden key in the lock, and to her great delight it fitted!

Alice opened the door and found that it led into a small passage, not much larger than a rat-hole: she knelt down and looked along the passage into the loveliest garden you ever saw. How she longed to get out of that dark hall, and wander about among those beds of bright flowers and those cool fountains, but she could not even get her head through the doorway; “and even if my head would go through,” thought poor Alice, “it would be of very little use without my shoulders. Oh, how I wish I could shut up like a telescope! I think I could, if I only knew how to begin.” For, you see, so many out-of-the-way things had happened lately, that Alice had begun to think that very few things indeed were really impossible.

questions.title: The last afternoon at the library
questions.passage:
When the council announced that the riverside library would close for six weeks of repairs, Maya worried about the people who used it every day. Her grandfather came for the newspapers, a neighbour used its computers to apply for work, and younger children gathered there on Thursdays to hear stories. A notice promised that borrowed books would not become overdue during the closure. It said nothing about where those other activities could happen.

Maya suggested a temporary library in the empty shop beside the bakery. Her friend Leo immediately began drawing a colourful sign. Their librarian, Mrs Shah, admired the drawing but asked them to look more closely at the building. The doorway had a high step, the only toilet was upstairs, and rain had left a dark patch on the ceiling. A cheerful sign would not solve those problems. Maya felt embarrassed until Mrs Shah explained that noticing a difficulty early was useful, not a failure.

The community centre offered a small room on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. It had a ramp, a ground-floor toilet and a reliable internet connection. However, it could hold only four shelves. The library had hundreds of shelves. Instead of choosing only their own favourite stories, Maya and Leo asked regular visitors what they needed. Several requested large-print books. Children wanted short stories and animal books. Adults asked for local newspapers and help using online forms.

The volunteers arranged a rotating collection. Readers could request a title on Tuesday and collect it on Thursday if it was available. A volunteer would bring the requested books from storage. Mrs Shah explained that requests were promises to try, not guarantees: somebody else might already have borrowed a title. Leo changed the sign so that it said “Ask us to find your next book” rather than “Every book, every day”.

On the last afternoon before the closure, Maya watched a volunteer load four empty shelves into a van. The temporary room would never contain everything the old library held. Yet the list of visitors who had offered to help was growing. Her grandfather had volunteered to welcome people at the door, and the neighbour who used the computers would help others fill in forms. Maya folded the request sheets and put them in her bag. The library, she realised, was larger than its building: some of its most useful resources could walk across the road by themselves.

questions.explanation: Temperature differences across the grounds
questions.title: A cooler playground
questions.passage:
At the start of the summer term, the science club investigated why some parts of the school grounds felt much hotter than others. Ayaan thought the black playground surface was responsible. Jess thought the most important difference was shade. Their teacher asked them to turn those ideas into questions that could be tested rather than voting for the explanation they preferred.

The club selected four places: black paving in sunlight, black paving beneath a tree, pale paving in sunlight and grass in sunlight. At each place they measured the surface temperature at noon on five dry days. They used the same instrument and waited the same length of time before recording a reading. They also wrote down whether clouds passed over the sun. One pupil wanted to take a reading at seven in the morning because the playground was quieter then. The group decided that changing the time would make that reading harder to compare with the others.

The black paving in sunlight was hottest on every day. The shaded black paving was much cooler. Pale paving in sunlight was usually cooler than unshaded black paving, but it was not always cooler than the grass. Both Ayaan and Jess had found part of the explanation. A dark surface could absorb more sunlight, while shade reduced the sunlight reaching any surface. The club had measured surface temperature, however, not the temperature of the surrounding air. The report needed to make that distinction clear.

The pupils proposed planting three trees beside the playground. The site manager pointed out that young trees would take years to provide much shade and would need watering while they became established. A shade sail might work sooner, but it would need secure supports and inspections after strong winds. Painting a surface a lighter colour could change its temperature, although the finish would also have to remain safe to walk on when wet.

Instead of naming a single perfect solution, the report compared short-term and long-term choices. It recommended a temporary shaded seating area while the school investigated suitable trees. It also proposed repeating the measurements in another season and taking air-temperature readings separately. During the presentation, a governor asked whether five days proved the playground would behave identically throughout the year. Ayaan said no. Their results supported a useful decision, but did not answer every question. Jess added the words “during our five-day investigation” to the headline on the display. The change made it less dramatic, and more accurate.

questions.title: The message in the harbour
questions.passage:
The fog arrived while Nora was helping her uncle mend a fishing net. Within minutes the far side of the harbour disappeared, followed by the red buoy near the entrance. The boat beneath them moved gently against its ropes. From somewhere beyond the wall came a low engine noise, then silence. Nora looked at the clock in the cabin. The supply boat was due in twenty minutes, but her uncle had already telephoned its skipper to warn him about the visibility.

A folded note lay under a mug on the bench. Nora had found it inside a tin while clearing a cupboard earlier that morning. The writing was faded, and a corner had torn away. She could read “When the light is gone, follow the bell”, followed by a name she did not recognise. It sounded like an instruction from an adventure story. Her uncle said the tin had belonged to his grandmother, who had kept old photographs and scraps from the harbour office.

Nora wanted to know whether the note described a hidden path. Instead of walking out alone into the fog, she photographed it and sent the image to the local history group. A member replied with a newspaper clipping from 1932. A storm had damaged the harbour lamp that winter. Until it was repaired, a keeper had rung a handbell at the end of the pier to guide people who were already close to shore. Another message explained that the keeper’s surname matched the faded name on the note.

The discovery made the words feel less mysterious, but not less interesting. Nora imagined somebody standing in cold spray, repeating the same motion until a small boat reached safety. Her uncle pointed out that the note belonged to a particular place and time. It was not sensible modern navigation advice. The present harbour used different signals, and in poor visibility crews followed current instructions and suitable equipment rather than a scrap from a cupboard.

The supply boat arrived nearly an hour late, after the fog began to lift. Nora watched its skipper secure the ropes before he unloaded anything. She put the old note in a clean folder and wrote down where she had found it, who had replied, and which details were still uncertain. Nobody could yet prove who had written the message or who was meant to receive it. The newspaper explained the bell, but not the entire story. That evening Nora returned to the history group’s page. This time she asked a narrower question: did anyone have a photograph of the harbour keeper from that winter?

questions.prompt: Demonstration question 31: which section are you reading?
questions.explanation: The class with the most car-free journeys
questions.title: Should every journey be counted?
questions.passage:
A student council wanted to encourage walking, cycling and public transport. Its first proposal was a competition: each pupil would record how they travelled to school, and the class with the highest number of car-free journeys would win a picnic. The idea seemed straightforward until the council invited comments from the rest of the school.

Some pupils lived close enough to walk along quiet streets. Others travelled from villages without an early bus. A pupil who used a wheelchair explained that the nearest accessible stop was much farther away than the ordinary stop shown on the route map. Another pupil was driven to school after taking a younger sibling to a nursery in the opposite direction. Counting every car journey as a failure would ignore these differences. It could also encourage pupils to hide information rather than discuss what would help them.

The council revised the plan. Instead of ranking children, it would gather anonymous information about journeys and barriers. A short survey would ask which options were realistically available and what changes people would find useful. Pupils could skip questions, and the results would be reported for the school as a whole. The council would not publish individual routes or addresses. It also decided that weather, safety and accessibility needed to be considered before suggesting that anyone change their journey.

One member objected that a survey would be less exciting than a competition. Another replied that excitement was not the only measure of success. If the school learned that a missing crossing stopped many families walking, it could raise a specific issue with the council responsible for roads. If secure cycle parking was the main problem, the school might be able to act itself. Accurate information could lead to improvements that a prize alone would never produce.

The final proposal still included a celebration, but nobody had to earn entry by choosing a particular form of transport. At the end of term the school would hold an outdoor breakfast and share what it had learned. The student council would report both successes and unresolved problems. It would also repeat a few survey questions later to see whether changes had made a difference. The aim had shifted from identifying the “best” travellers to making better choices possible for more people. That was a quieter ambition, but the pupils thought it was a fairer one.

questions.title: An archive with gaps
questions.passage:
In a box of donated photographs, a museum volunteer found two pictures of the same town square. Both showed a fountain, a row of shops and a tram line. On the back of one, somebody had written “Market day, 1911”. The second had no date. Its buildings looked cleaner, and several shop signs had changed. The volunteer suggested that the second picture must have been taken later. Curator Dr Ellis agreed that this was possible, but asked what other explanations might fit the evidence.

A photograph records a view, not a complete account. The darker image might have been printed differently or stored in worse conditions. A shop could change its sign and then change it back. A date written on a photograph might describe the scene accurately, or it might have been added much later by someone guessing. None of these possibilities made the pictures worthless. They showed why a confident label needed support from more than one clue.

The museum team compared the images with street directories and a map showing when the tram route opened. The route had begun operating in 1908, so neither photograph could show an operating tram on that line before that year. A directory listed a bakery at the corner address in 1910 and a pharmacy there in 1914. Unfortunately, the years between those editions were missing. The sign in the second photograph looked like the pharmacy’s name, but part of it was hidden by an awning.

An older catalogue described a fountain repair in 1913. A decorative stone visible in the first picture was absent from the second. That detail supported the later-date theory, yet the team still could not assign an exact year. Perhaps the stone had been removed temporarily before the recorded repair. Dr Ellis wrote a provisional label: “Probably after 1913; exact date uncertain.” She added the reasons in the collection notes so that a future researcher could check them.

When the photographs appeared in an exhibition, visitors were invited to contribute information. One supplied a family postcard showing the same pharmacy, postmarked 1915. It strengthened the interpretation without proving that the museum’s photograph was taken in that year. Another visitor said the uncertainty made the display seem unfinished. The volunteer replied that showing the limits of knowledge was part of telling the story honestly. A gap in the archive was not an invitation to invent a detail.
